name: 01_history
title: The annual temperature cycle dominates the history
question: What patterns must a model represent?
scope: 2011 through September 16, 2021, before the first development origin.
finding: 93,887 expected hourly slots; 93,712 usable temperatures. Warm and cold seasons repeat, with substantial daily variation.
implication: Use calendar and hour features. Compare training seasons using matched September backtests.
limitation: Daily means describe hourly reports, not continuous daily extrema. Partial 2021 is not compared as a complete year.

name: 02_missingness
title: Quality exclusions and missing observations
question: Are there gaps that affect lags, fitting, or scoring?
scope: Training scope only; absent or quarantined targets counted as unavailable.
finding: 175 unavailable hours (0.186%); longest consecutive run is 12 hours.
implication: Keep the hourly grid, retain quality flags, and score only available targets on a shared mask.
limitation: Gray/empty cells after the 2021 cutoff were not analyzed; unavailable includes source disagreements, not just absent reports.

name: 03_months
title: All months provide more examples, but different temperature regimes
question: Why not choose all months purely because there are more rows?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F.
finding: September mean is 72.5°F; January 41.6°F and July 80.1°F.
implication: Aug–Oct is the initial candidate because it brackets September. Retain all months to test whether season-aware modeling improves September errors.
limitation: Boxes show quartiles and whiskers; hidden outlier markers are retained in data. Row count does not equal independent weather episodes.

name: 04_season_distributions
title: The target fortnight sits within a changing autumn distribution
question: How representative are neighboring months?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F.
finding: Historical target-window median 70.0°F; middle 80% spans 59.0–81.0°F.
implication: Neighboring months add examples of fronts and daily cycles, but month/day features must represent the autumn cooling.
limitation: These are descriptive historical quantiles, not calibrated forecast intervals for 2026.

name: 05_month_hour
title: The daily cycle changes with season
question: Should hour and season interact?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F.
finding: The warmest average hours occur in the afternoon; nights and mornings are cooler. Seasonal means and daily ranges differ.
implication: Use cyclic hour/day-of-year features and consider hour-by-season interactions in linear regression.
limitation: Civil-hour grouping respects DST; it is not an elapsed-time lag. Means conceal cloudy, wet, and frontal regimes.

name: 06_daily_cycle
title: Weather variation is wider than the average daily cycle
question: How much variation does a calendar-only forecast miss?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F.
finding: September mean cycle range is 15.1°F, peaking at civil hour 15.
implication: Calendar averages are useful baselines; forecast weather inputs may explain departures.
limitation: Shaded 10th–90th percentiles are weather dispersion, not uncertainty in the mean or forecast coverage.

name: 07_autumn_transition
title: The forecast window is part of an autumn cooling transition
question: Is September interchangeable with August and October?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F.
finding: Average temperature declines through the candidate season; individual years depart considerably from that pattern.
implication: Use continuous calendar features rather than assigning one September constant.
limitation: Smoothing is descriptive and uses neighboring training days; it is not a forecast and is not applied across evaluation cutoffs.

name: 08_target_weather
title: Ten historical Septembers show different two-week weather paths
question: How variable is the exact target fortnight?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F.
finding: 3,355 usable target-like hours represent only ten annual fortnights.
implication: Validate whole 336-hour forecasts at historical origins; random hourly splitting would share weather events across train and test.
limitation: Training-era examples are descriptive; 2021–2025 evaluation fortnight outcomes are not plotted here.

name: 09_recency
title: Year-to-year weather complicates a short-record warming estimate
question: How should environmental change affect history selection?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F.
finding: The descriptive September slope is +2.74°F/decade (slope SE 2.69); only ten yearly means support it.
implication: Compare five- and ten-year histories on matched September folds. Do not select a start year as an assumed climate break or add an arbitrary warming correction.
limitation: Night/afternoon groups are proxies, not observed daily minima/maxima. Ten years cannot isolate global warming, urban development, station changes, or circulation effects.

name: 10_history_sensitivity
title: History length changes the estimated seasonal baseline
question: Does using less history visibly change the baseline?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F.
finding: Five- vs ten-year target-window hourly means differ by 1.99°F on average in absolute value.
implication: This motivates a backtest comparison; it does not establish which window forecasts better.
limitation: This is the 2021-origin comparison. The final 2026 ten-year candidate is 2016–2025; its optimality has not been established.

name: 11_lag_dependence
title: Recent temperatures are informative, but dependence changes with horizon
question: How far does recent-weather dependence persist?
scope: Core pre-2021-origin history; both ends of each pair must fall in Aug–Oct.
finding: Calendar-demeaned lag correlations: 24h 0.64; 168h 0.03; 336h -0.03.
implication: At a fixed origin, future lags must be recursively predicted or replaced by origin-known summaries. Never feed observed target-window lags into later forecast hours.
limitation: These pairwise descriptive correlations are not forecast skill. Calendar means are calculated in the same training sample; no significance bands assume independent hours.

name: 12_feature_relationships
title: Same-hour weather relationships require an availability check
question: Which variables relate to temperature, and can they be used?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F. Aug–Oct only.
finding: Temperature/dew-point correlation is 0.74; temperature/RH -0.43.
implication: Use observations only as origin-known summaries. Future weather features must come from frozen pre-origin forecasts; RH is also mathematically related to temperature and dew point.
limitation: Associations combine daily/seasonal cycles and weather effects; they are not causal effects or evidence of incremental predictive value.

name: 13_feature_availability
title: Observation fields have different completeness and meanings
question: What cleaning is needed before feature engineering?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F. Aug–Oct only.
finding: Availability varies by field; target screening and covariate missingness have different causes.
implication: Fit any imputation only on each training fold; retain trace-rain and variable-wind flags. Do not fill missing wind direction with north or empty cloud layers with an invented cloud amount.
limitation: Numeric precipitation blanks may mean no reported amount, not confirmed zero. Some calm METARs have blank parsed speed; preserve originals pending explicit parsing rules.

name: 14_lagged_features
title: Observed inputs have a horizon-dependent relationship with temperature
question: Do same-hour relationships persist for a two-week forecast?
scope: Core Aug–Oct pairs; temperature has training month/hour mean removed.
finding: The table reports exact-time associations at 1, 6, 24, 72, 168 and 336 hours, with the number of available pairs.
implication: Test origin-known weather summaries; do not assume same-hour correlations imply 14-day usefulness.
limitation: Predictor calendar patterns are not removed. These associations are exploratory; only out-of-sample comparisons can establish useful features.

name: 15_cloud_regimes
title: Cloud categories accompany different daytime and nighttime regimes
question: Should clouds be treated as a simple ordered numeric feature?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F. Aug–Oct only; first reported cloud layer.
finding: Mean temperature departures differ by cloud category and time of day; category sample counts are supplied.
implication: If used, encode observed categories explicitly; future cloud features must be forecast values, with their own representation.
limitation: The first layer does not measure total cloud cover. Weather regimes confound associations, and categories with small counts are unstable.

name: 16_source_precision
title: Two archives verify the same observations; precision is a separate issue
question: Do archive agreement and displayed precision justify treating all values as exact?
scope: Core pre-2021-origin reports; paired values only.
finding: 93,655 IEM/T-group pairs; median absolute difference 0.040°F; 37 core targets are quarantined.
implication: Keep raw values, quality codes, provenance and alternate precision. Resolve target definitions before any final scoring.
limitation: IEM and NOAA share airport observations and are not independent sensors. Parsed T-group temperature must never be used as a predictor of the same temperature target.

name: 17_event_context
title: A September 2018 event illustrates a changing weather regime
question: Should unusual weather be removed as an outlier?
scope: September 10–19, 2018, training history surrounding Hurricane Florence.
finding: Temperature and pressure evolve together across this event; unusually persistent weather is part of the forecasting problem.
implication: Retain physically plausible extremes and events. Flag source errors separately from rare weather.
limitation: This plot does not attribute every fluctuation to the hurricane, and hourly samples are not true continuous extrema.

name: 18_contiguous_decomposition
title: A continuous training segment separates daily cycle and slower change
question: Can daily structure be separated without filling gaps?
finding: STL separates a repeating 24-hour component, a smooth trend, and residual weather variation.
implication: This supports explicit daily-cycle features; it is a descriptive diagnostic, not a fitted forecast.
limitation: The two-sided smoother is training-only. One segment and a chosen 24-hour period do not establish the optimal model. DST is handled in elapsed UTC hours.

name: 19_residual_pacf
title: Residual dependence remains after descriptive decomposition
question: Does removing a daily cycle make hours independent?
scope: Same 1257-hour gap-free 2020 training segment.
finding: The PACF reports remaining short-lag dependence conditional on intermediate lags.
implication: Use time-respecting validation and weather-event/year-level uncertainty summaries.
limitation: This segment is not a model-selection test. No confidence bands are shown because iid-hour assumptions are inappropriate.

name: 20_2026_known_context
title: Weather known before the final forecast origin
question: What does the latest permissible station history look like?
scope: August 1–September 16, 2026 only; separate from the initial model-design EDA.
finding: 1,128 known-hour slots; mean departure from the 2011–2020 calendar/hour reference is +3.45°F.
implication: Origin-known recent-weather summaries are candidates for later models.
limitation: A few weeks of weather are not evidence of a climate shift; no September 17–30, 2026 observations were accessed.

name: 21_frozen_forecast_input
title: A complete pre-origin GFS trajectory covers the required 336 hours
question: Do the selected forecast and climatology sources cover every required hour?
scope: Forecast inputs for Sep 17 00:00–Sep 30 23:00 Raleigh civil time; no final observed outcomes.
finding: All 336 GFS temperature values and 336 normal lookups are present; 225 GFS target slots fall after native hourly resolution ends.
implication: This is a candidate forecast input/baseline, not the project prediction. Preserve issuance, lead time and interpolation flags.
limitation: GFS is gridded and one forecast trajectory supplies no calibrated uncertainty. Normals use local standard time (UTC−5), correctly offset from September EDT (UTC−4). Routine-report :51 scoring still needs agreed alignment.

name: 22_gfs_calibration_diagnostic
title: Frozen GFS error varies across the two-week horizon
question: Is raw forecast guidance equally accurate at every lead?
scope: Calibration-only April 2–July 23, 2026 initializations; July 30 and August confirmation runs excluded.
finding: 17 origins; 5,700 scored forecast/report pairs. Pooled MAE 5.69°F, RMSE 7.69°F, bias -1.98°F.
implication: Consider lead-dependent calibration later, and compare candidates on the same origins and observation mask. This analysis fits no correction.
limitation: An exploratory routine-report benchmark: interpolate the same frozen run to each actual :51 report timestamp. Weekly valid windows overlap, so pairs are not independent. Spring/summer errors are not September or final-project scores. Historical API publication times were not individually logged.

name: 23_rain_regimes
title: Trace rain, explicit zero and missing amounts have different meanings
question: Can precipitation be reduced to a simple missing-equals-zero rule?
scope: Complete training years 2011–2020; RDU routine reports; screened temperature in °F. Aug–Oct only.
finding: The table distinguishes positive measured precipitation, trace, explicit numeric zero, and no numeric amount, with counts and temperature associations.
implication: Retain trace and missing indicators; use rainfall as an origin-known summary or forecast input only after its reporting convention is explicit.
limitation: These are contemporaneous associations, not a causal rain effect or a forecast test. A missing numeric amount does not establish dry weather.

name: 24_archive_agreement
title: Exact-timestamp archive comparisons separate rounding from disagreements
question: How consistent is the airport temperature target across the two archives?
scope: Matched IEM/NOAA reports strictly before the first September 2021 origin.
finding: 93,754 matched reports; median absolute archive difference 0.040°F; 37 require review.
implication: Preserve source codes and match actual timestamps. Review disagreements instead of silently averaging archives or assuming displayed precision is accuracy.
limitation: Histogram omits quarantined pairs but their counts are reported. Both archives derive from the same station; later archive revisions cannot be proven to match what was distributed historically.
